sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: Front matter and abstract for Egami and Shin (MIT), 'Debiased Inference for AI-Generated Data without Gold-Standard Labels: Identification via Multiple Imperfect Measurements' (arXiv:2608.18294v2). Treating AI-measured variables as error-free biases downstream inference even above 90% accuracy, while existing corrections (DSL, PPI) require costly gold-standard labels. The authors propose debiased inference with multiple imperfect measurements (DMM), which combines three or more error-prone AI annotations under conditional independence given the latent true label and observed unit-level features (such as text embeddings), proves consistency and asymptotic normality via semiparametric inference theory, and introduces diagnostics for the conditional independence assumption.

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Section 1 (Introduction) and Related Literature. Motivates how non-random, nonclassical errors in AI/LLM annotations bias downstream social-science regressions and harm replicability, and contrasts gold-standard validation methods (DSL, PPI, MAR-S) with the proposed DMM framework, which uses three or more imperfect proxies without gold-standard labels. Summarizes three main contributions—replacing gold-standard labels via conditional CP decomposition given the latent label and rich unit covariates, general moment-estimator applicability for categorical independent or dependent variables with J >= 3 proxies, and LLM-specific design and diagnostic strategies—before situating DMM relative to the AI-generated data, repeated-measurement identification (Kruskal, Hu, Allman–Matias–Rhodes, Dawid–Skene), and proxy-based causal inference literatures.

sections.extract: One of the most common applications of AI in the social sciences has been in measurement. Re- searchers have used AI to measure a wide range of variables, such as sentiment, tone, topics (e.g., Gilardi, Alizadeh and Kubli, 2023; Ziems et al., 2024), protests, political violence (e.g., Halterman and Keith, 2026), and job types (e.g., Hansen et al., 2023), among others. Such measurement tasks are only the first step.

sections.title: The Problem Setting and Existing Approaches

summary.text: Section 2 opening (The Problem Setting and Existing Approaches). Notes that ignoring measurement error in machine or human annotations biases downstream analysis even when annotation accuracy exceeds 90%, and states that Section 2 and Section 3 first focus on a binary error-prone independent variable before Section 4 generalizes to multicategory independent or dependent variables.

sections.extract: Scholars often use machine or human annotations to measure key variables of interest that they want to analyze in downstream analysis. However, as recent papers theoretically and empirically show, 5 ignoring measurement errors in the annotation step can bias downstream inference, even when the accuracy of the annotation step is high, e.g., more than 90%. sections.title: Setup

summary.text: Section 2.1 (Setup). Formalizes the binary latent independent variable setting: for n units with unobserved true label X*_i in {0,1}, observed outcome Y_i, covariates W_i, and J >= 3 binary proxy labels X^(j)_i, the target parameter beta* uniquely solves the full-data moment equation E[psi_F(Y, X*, W; beta)] = 0. Illustrates psi_F for linear, logistic, and generalized linear models and notes that under model misspecification beta* represents the population projection parameter.

sections.title: Naive Approaches Ignoring Measurement Errors

summary.text: Section 2.2.1 (Naive Approaches Ignoring Measurement Errors). Shows that collapsing J proxy labels into a single index X-check (such as majority voting) and plugging it directly into the downstream moment equation yields a population moment bias E[(X-check - X*){psi_F(Y,1,W;beta) - psi_F(Y,0,W;beta)}], which remains nonzero even at high classification accuracy because classification errors are nonclassical and correlated with downstream variables.

sections.title: Gold-Standard-Only Estimation

summary.text: Section 2.2.2 (Gold-Standard-Only Estimation). Defines the inverse-probability-weighted gold-standard-only (GSO) estimator using units sampled for expert labeling with known researcher-controlled probabilities rho_i = Pr(R_i = 1 | Y_i, W_i, X-tilde_i). Notes that GSO is consistent and asymptotically normal for beta* but inefficient because it discards the proxy labels and all unlabeled units.

sections.extract: To address non-random, nonclassical measurement errors, the most dominant existing approach is to rely on gold-standard labels. Such methods assume that X∗ i is observed for a small subset of units sampled according to a known sampling design. sections.title: Debiased Inference with Gold-Standard Labels

summary.text: Section 2.2.3 (Debiased Inference with Gold-Standard Labels). Reviews prediction-and-correction estimators (DSL, PPI, MAR-S) that combine large-scale proxy predictions with a gold-standard validation sample, presenting the cross-fitted doubly robust DSL moment function as a benchmark. Explains that DSL achieves unbiasedness for the oracle moment under a known sampling design without assumptions on LLM error structure, and contrasts the continuum of naive, GSO, and validation-based bias-correction approaches.

sections.extract: More recently, a broad class of methods combines predictions available at scale with a smaller sample of gold-standard measurements to bias-correct downstream analysis. This class of bias-correction methods includes design-based supervised learning (DSL; Egami et al., 2023, 2026), prediction- powered inference (PPI; Angelopoulos et al., 2023), methods reviewed in Ludwig, Mullainathan and Rambachan (2026), MAR-S

sections.title: Debiased Inference with Multiple Imperfect Measurements

summary.text: Section 3 opening and Section 3.1 (Assumptions). Reviews the classical conditional independence assumption X^(1) _||_ ... _||_ X^(J) | X* from the latent-class literature and explains why it fails when human or LLM annotators share input-driven or prompt-driven error sources. Introduces Assumption 3.1, which conditions on both the latent label X* and observed covariates D-tilde = (D, W, Y)—including task features such as text embeddings or prompt metadata—so misclassification rates can vary across both annotators and units.

sections.title: Identification of Conditional Classification Rates

summary.text: Section 3.2.1 (Identification of Conditional Classification Rates). Adapts Allman, Matias, and Rhodes (2009) Theorem 4 and Kruskal's (1977) uniqueness theorem by partitioning the J >= 3 proxies into three nonempty subsets to form a three-way conditional probability tensor with a two-component CP decomposition. Shows that when each subset contains at least one informative proxy, Kruskal's rank condition k_1 + k_2 + k_3 >= 6 holds with equality, and combining this with an anchoring rule (such as eta*_{j+,1} > eta*_{j+,0}) uniquely identifies the mixing probabilities and all conditional classification rates eta*_{j,a}(d) (Result 1).

summary.text: Section 3.2.2 (Identification via the Robust Bridge Function). Proves Proposition 3.1 showing that H^R is unbiased for X* and has only second- and third-order conditional bias in cross-fitted first-stage nuisance errors (yielding O_p(delta_n^2) remainder), and proves Theorem 3.1 establishing identification of beta* via the DMM moment equation.

sections.title: Estimation and Inference

summary.text: Section 3.3 (Estimation and Inference). Defines the K-fold cross-fitted DMM estimator beta-hat_DMM using out-of-fold nuisance estimates (e.g., via EM or sieve methods) and proves Theorem 3.2: beta-hat_DMM is consistent when J - 1 proxy nuisance models converge (multiple robustness) and root-n asymptotically normal when nuisance errors converge at rate o_p(n^{-1/4}), with a plug-in sandwich variance estimator. Analyzes asymptotic efficiency as a function of proxy count J and single-bridge variances kappa_{j,a}(d), showing an O(J^{-2}) bridge-variance reduction under homogeneous proxies and noting that adding a very noisy proxy can increase variance unless it passes an explicit variance threshold.

sections.extract: Given the identification results in the previous section, this section proposes the DMM (debiased inference with multiple imperfect measurements) estimator and proves its consistency and asymptotic normality. First, to estimate the conditional classification rate, we use cross-fitting (Chernozhukov et al., 2018) and separate estimation of the nuisance function from evaluation of the downstream moment function.

sections.title: Multicategory Labels

summary.text: Section 4.2 (Multicategory Labels). Extends DMM to a K*-category latent variable with J >= 3 proxies of potentially differing category counts K_j by defining class-specific bridge functions H_a(Y-tilde, D-tilde) via the left inverse S^+(d) of the conditional measurement matrix S(d) and combining single-proxy bridges into the Neyman-orthogonal robust bridge H^R_a = 3 H_{2,a} - 2 H_{3,a}. Discusses Kruskal rank conditions (3K* >= 2K* + 2 when three proxy groups have full column rank K*), composite proxy grouping when individual proxies have fewer than K* categories, anchoring across all K* classes, and uniform lower bounds on the smallest singular value sigma_min{S_j(d)}.

sections.title: Designing and Assessing Conditional Independence

summary.text: Section 5 opening (Designing and Assessing Conditional Independence). Emphasizes that conditional independence of measurement errors is a structural assumption not guaranteed by high proxy accuracy, and previews the three parts of Section 5: measurement design (Section 5.1), gold-standard-free diagnostics (Section 5.2), and direct testing plus DMM-assisted DSL bias correction when a small validation sample is available (Section 5.3).

sections.extract: Conditional independence is a structural assumption about the residual errors of the measurements and is not guaranteed by high predictive accuracy of each imperfect measurement. We therefore first recommend explicitly designing multiple measurements to make the assumption as plausible as possible (Section 5.1). We then propose a diagnostic tool for the conditional independence assumption (Section 5.2). We finally

sections.title: Making the Conditional Independence Assumption More Plausible

summary.text: Section 5.1 (Making the Conditional Independence Assumption More Plausible). Recommends three practical strategies for LLM and human annotation designs: (1) enriching the conditioning set D-tilde with input features (text length, style, embeddings, or cross-LLM disagreement scores as task-difficulty proxies); (2) partitioning annotators into G >= 3 conditionally independent groups across distinct model families (e.g., GPT, Claude, open-weight LLMs, and blinded humans) while allowing arbitrary within-group error dependence; and (3) randomizing or recording prompt versions across annotators to prevent prompt-induced error correlation.

sections.extract: The first approach is to judiciously create a conditioning set. Unlike the traditional conditional independence assumption that only conditions on the latent variable itself (equation (3.1)), our method explicitly allows for conditioning on auxiliary input- or annotation-level information Di and the downstream variables Wi. sections.title: Diagnostics Without Gold-Standard Labels

summary.text: Section 5.2 (Diagnostics Without Gold-Standard Labels). Notes that three binary proxies with two latent classes are just-identified (7 degrees of freedom and 7 parameters), whereas J >= 4 proxies yield 2^J - 2J - 2 overidentifying restrictions at each covariate value d. Proposes two gold-standard-free specification diagnostics: goodness-of-fit / conditional moment tests comparing the fitted product-mixture distribution to the empirical joint label distribution, and multiplier-bootstrap stability tests comparing DMM parameter estimates across distinct subsets of three or more proxies.

sections.title: Testing and Bias-Correction with Small Gold-Standard Data

summary.text: Section 5.3 (Testing and Bias-Correction with Small Gold-Standard Data). Shows how a small validation sample with known sampling probabilities rho_i enables (1) a direct conditional moment test of zero residual products across proxy subsets given X* = a and D-tilde, and (2) a DMM-assisted DSL estimator that uses the cross-fitted DMM moment function as a full-sample imputation / control variate corrected by inverse-probability-weighted validation residuals, guaranteeing validity even if conditional independence fails while improving precision when DMM is informative.

sections.extract: When the conditional independence assumption is in serious doubt, it is generally recommended to collect the gold-standard labels, even for a small amount of data, for two reasons: (a) direct testing of the conditional independence assumption and (b) bias correction without assuming the conditional independence assumption. sections.title: Simulation Study: Platform Differences in Political Advertising Tone

summary.text: Section 6.1 (Simulation Study: Platform Differences in Political Advertising Tone). Evaluates DMM over 500 Monte Carlo replications calibrated to 12,973 ads from Fowler et al. (2021), estimating the Facebook coefficient (target 1.314) in a logistic regression for the binary Promote indicator as J increases from 3 to 15 F1-ranked proxies. Reports that with the top 3 proxies naive majority voting suffers severe bias (0.186) and near-zero 95% CI coverage (0.018), whereas DMM eliminates bias (0.002), achieves nominal coverage (0.948), cuts RMSE by two thirds (0.063 vs. 0.191), and approaches the infeasible oracle RMSE (0.045) as informative proxies are added.

sections.title: Empirical Validation: Accusations of Wrongdoing in China

summary.text: Section 6.2 (Empirical Validation: Accusations of Wrongdoing in China) and Figure 1 captions/labels. Evaluates DMM on 1,412 real citizen complaints from Pan and Chen (2018) using three LLM proxies (GPT-4.1 5-shot, GPT-4 5-shot, Llama-4 0-shot) for the latent prefecture-level wrongdoing regressor in a logistic regression of upward reporting (expert benchmark -1.039). Shows that single-proxy naive estimates are heavily biased (-1.869 to -0.388, coverage 0.154-0.572), while DMM without any expert labels yields -0.844 with 0.862 resample coverage, comparable to DSL using 500 expert labels (-1.279, coverage 0.981).

Specifies the shared parametric logistic latent-class nuisance model used in both applications, modeling latent prevalence Pr(L*_i = 1 | Z_i) = expit(Z_i^T alpha) and class-specific proxy response probabilities Pr(L^(j)_i = 1 | L*_i = a, Z_i) = expit(Z_i^T gamma_{j,a}) without including the downstream outcome Y_i in the Pan-Chen measurement likelihood.

sections.title: Expectation–Maximization Algorithm

summary.text: Appendix C.2.1 (Expectation-Maximization Algorithm). Details the E-step log-sum-exp posterior responsibility update xi^(t)_i and M-step fractional/weighted logistic regressions for fitting the latent-class nuisance model, along with Table C.1's shared numerical settings (6 starts, 500 max iterations, 10^{-5} responsibility tolerance, 10^{-7} log-likelihood tolerance, [-20,20] coefficient clipping, [10^{-8}, 1-10^{-8}] probability clipping, and 0.05 bridge denominator floor) and post-EM sign orientation.

sections.title: Monte Carlo Simulations

summary.text: Appendix C.3 (Monte Carlo Simulations). Documents the full calibration and evaluation protocol for the Fowler et al. (2021) simulation study (12,973 ads, Promote prevalence 0.756, target Facebook logit coefficient 1.3141, 500 replications per nested proxy count J, random tie-breaking for even-J majority vote) and summarizes additional simulations for the lower-prevalence Contrast (17.2%, target -1.029) and Attack (7.1%, target -1.334) tone indicators.

sections.extract: Data, annotation task, and downstream target. The annotation task follows the Wesleyan Media Project codebook used in Fowler et al. (2021): an ad is classified according to whether its primary purpose is to promote a candidate, attack a candidate, or contrast candidates. sections.title: Empirical Validation

summary.text: Appendix C.4 (Empirical Validation) and Tables C.2-C.3. Presents Table C.2 (Fowler simulation results for Attack and Contrast outcomes showing near-zero DMM bias and 0.942-0.962 coverage versus severe naive bias and undercoverage) and Table C.3 (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and weighted/positive F1 for the three LLM proxies in Pan and Chen 2018), and documents the 1,412-complaint logistic specification, the 500-label generalized-random-forest DSL benchmark, and the 500-draw nonparametric bootstrap coverage diagnostic.

sections.extract: Data and downstream model. The analysis uses 1,412 Chinese citizen complaints. The la- tent independent variable is the expert-coded indicator X∗ i = 1{prefecture-level wrongdoing}, and the downstream outcome Yi = SendOrNoti indicates whether the complaint was sent to higher-level authorities.
